articles.title: Jensen Huang Espionage Allegations Threaten Nvidia Federal Defense Contracts
articles.content: LivestreamMenuThe allegations against Jensen Huang have brought new attention to the Nvidia CEO's potential influence over U.S. policy on chip sales to China.Lawmakers are looking to investigate Nvidia's China ties."In 35 years, I haven't seen a chip CEO with this much direct influence on export policy," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO at Moor Insights & Strategy.In this article Following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's admission on Sunday to an extramarital affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, the chipmaker's relationship to China is about to come under intense scrutiny in Washington, D.C. Since October 2022, when the Biden administration announced sweeping controls to limit China's ability to obtain advanced U.S. chips, Nvidia has seen its business diminish in the world's second-largest economy. Months after an even stricter set of rules was implemented by the Trump administration, Huang said in October 2025, "We are 100% out of China." The recent allegations against Huang, while throwing the chipmaker into crisis, have also brought attention to the Nvidia CEO's potential influence over U.S. policy on chip sales to China, where its business once flourished. Of particular interest is whether restricted Nvidia chips have reached Chinese companies through customers like Singapore-based Megaspeed, the company linked to Alice Huang. The New York Times first reported that the Chinese businesswoman was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, according to people briefed on the intelligence circulated in a memo among the Trump administration in the spring. China has called the allegation a smear. Jensen Huang has been closely aligned with President Donald Trump during his second administration, helping advise the White House on artificial intelligence safety regulations, while also pushing for looser restrictions on selling AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia would be allowed to ship its H200 chips to China, provided the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales. In March, Huang told reporters that Nvidia had "received purchase orders, and we're in the process of restarting our manufacturing." Huang was a last-minute addition to the roster of tech executives who joined Trump on a trip to China in May, after the president was briefed on intelligence concerns, according to the Times. "In 35 years, I haven't seen a chip CEO with this much direct influence on export policy," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO at Moor Insights & Strategy, in an email. Since last week's midterm elections that included sweeping victories across the country for Democrats, the mood in Washington has changed. Three House committees have requested closed-door briefings with the Nvidia CEO about his relationship with Megaspeed. Democratic lawmakers, who are about to take power in the House and Senate, have said publicly that Congress will investigate and seek answers. Trump said Monday that he was "amazed" by the allegations and that Huang told him he "had no idea that she was a spy." The FBI is now looking into the issue, Trump said at a White House briefing. It's been a long four years for Nvidia in China. Before the initial export controls in 2022, China made up nearly a quarter of Nvidia's revenue. Nvidia responded to the Biden-era restrictions by redesigning some of its products to comply with the new regulations. "It was a turbulent month or so as the company went upside down to re-engineer" the products, Huang told CNBC in a 2023 interview. Still, he was confident the company could continue selling chips to China. "I think we're going to be just fine in the ability to serve the customers there," he said. After the Biden administration tightened export restrictions again, Nvidia redesigned another AI graphics processing unit for China, the H20. Following reports that Chinese model developer DeepSeek was using restricted Nvidia chips, the Trump administration limited sales of H20. Nvidia revealed it would incur $5.5 billion in costs related to canceled orders for the redesigned chip. However, despite saying in its forecasts that "we're assuming 0% for China," the company maintained business in the region. In the last fiscal year, Nvidia reported that about 9% of its revenue came from China, including Hong Kong, although that includes revenue from segments outside of restricted data center chips, such as gaming, auto and industrial. Nvidia's China revenue was 8% in the most recent quarter. A report in May from short seller Culper Research alleged Nvidia's China exposure was much higher. The firm said that more than 20% of Nvidia's fiscal 2026 compute revenue was driven by China, supported by "illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries," according to the report. A loophole allows Chinese companies to rent Nvidia GPUs in data centers, even when they're restricted from buying them outright. For example, a Chinese company could lease Nvidia computing power in Europe by renting server capacity from a non-Chinese neocloud or data center operator that's exempt from export controls. Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment for this story. Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer based in Singapore, has been accused of diverting its own supply of Nvidia's restricted AI chips to Chinese companies. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and said inspections found no evidence of violations. In 2025, Nvidia changed the way it reported regional sales to categorize by customer headquarters, instead of by where the products were billed. Nvidia also stopped reporting Singapore sales during the same period. "Whether Blackwell chips reached China is a Megaspeed question that predates this week," said Moorhead, pointing to Bloomberg reporting in December 2025 that found Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more Nvidia chips than Nvidia tallied in its data centers. In 2025, a House Select Committee opened an investigation into whether China's DeepSeek operates on Nvidia's chips. A separate investigation by the U.S. Commerce Department was centered on Megaspeed. That probe was abruptly transferred to the Justice Department, the Times reported, following an email from Nvidia's general counsel to the Commerce Department seeking information about the investigation. The restrictions aren't just coming from the U.S. China has continued to limit the amount of Nvidia chips it will allow into the country, keeping Nvidia's China sales numbers down. The U.S. has licensed H200 sales to Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, but Beijing hasn't approved large-scale imports, Moorhead told CNBC. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July. Moorhead expects more export control legislation to pass as a result of the latest turmoil. Proposals could allow Congress oversight of chip export licenses or require chipmakers to install security mechanisms to track the location of chips to determine if they've found their way to China. "Every China license now gets read through this story," Moorhead said. "Jensen has been Nvidia's lead voice on China, and that voice is weaker." — CNBC's Kif Leswing and Seema Mody contributed reporting to this report. Correction: Three House committees have requested closed-door briefings with the Nvidia CEO about his relationship with Megaspeed. An earlier version misstated the time element. articles.title: US Soldier Arrested in Britain for Russian Cyber Espionage
articles.content: Image source, GoogleImage caption, The BBC understands the man was based at Imjin Barracks in Gloucestershire A soldier in the US Army has been arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia, British counter-terror police have said. The 41-year-old senior serviceman was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday. Counter Terrorism Policing London said the man had been arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023. Section one of the Act relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while section three relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service. As part of the investigation, officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire. The BBC understands the soldier was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire. The barracks serve as the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC), a strategic operational base for the alliance. Counter Terrorism Policing said it was not linked to any other ongoing investigations. FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement: "This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies." He added: "While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners." Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, from Counter Terrorism Policing London, described the arrest as "significant". "The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," she said. The unnamed soldier is currently in custody at a London police station. He has been detained under the National Security Act 2023, allowing police to hold him without charge for up to 14 days. Brig Gen Sean Stinchon, commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, said: "The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent. "I encourage anyone who thinks they've witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office." Additional reporting by Daniel Sandford, UK correspondent.

articles.title: Treasury Nominee Bessent Outlines Aggressive Bifurcated US-China Tech Doctrine
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will travel to China next week for US President Donald Trump’s third meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in 2026. PHOTO: REUTERS Published Nov 11, 2026, 09:28 AM Updated Nov 11, 2026, 12:38 PM Set as preferred source Listen Summarise US and China will keep competing on AI, but Scott Bessent said they must work together to reduce risks and avoid misunderstandings. A new Shenzhen dialogue on “superintelligence” will share testing methods and create a direct alert channel for serious AI incidents. Bessent also said trade ties will continue through tariff cuts, farm purchases and investment talks, while the US aims to “de-risk, not to decouple”. AI generated NEW YORK – The US and China should harbour no illusions about their differences on artificial intelligence as they navigate cooperation to mitigate the technology’s risks while competing for AI supremacy, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Nov 10. Bessent, who will travel to China next week for US President Donald Trump’s third meeting in 2026 with Chinese President Xi Jinping, said in prepared remarks to the National Committee on US-China Relations in New York that he wanted to "build a constructive relationship on the basis of balance and reciprocity”. The meeting in Shenzhen, to be held on the sidelines of the Nov 18 to 19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders summit, will advance a new bilateral dialogue on “superintelligence”, or SI, Bessent said, using the Trump administration’s preferred term for the technology. The dialogue is meant to guard against shared risks and “prevent a misunderstanding between our two systems”, he added. “We also expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release, and for keeping human judgment firmly in command of this technology,” Bessent said, adding that the two sides had agreed to establish a direct channel for alerting each other to serious incidents. Trump and Xi agreed on the new AI alert system during their previous meeting at the White House in September, but Trump at the time also said he was reluctant to add new guardrails because he wanted to preserve US leadership. “As SI advances, so will the need to engage in new areas of risk management – and to demonstrate how two nations can reconcile the demands of competition with the responsibilities of leadership,” Bessent said. “As we do so, we should harbour no illusions about the differences between the United States and China. As I stated earlier, our interests will not always coincide. And our approach to every challenge, likewise, will not always converge,” he added. Bessent’s remarks made no mention of the controversy surrounding Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. He is facing an investigation by the AI chipmaker’s board after a New York Times report that he had an affair with a businesswoman suspected by US security services of being a Chinese intelligence asset. China’s Foreign Ministry has called the spying accusations “groundless” and “a smear”. Nvidia has said its board has no reason to believe US national security or company secrets were compromised and that Huang has committed to cooperating with the internal review. Huang has told employees that he was unfaithful to his wife, but has provided no details about the relationship. While Huang was present at the Trump-Xi summits in Beijing in May and in Washington in September, it was unclear whether Trump would bring him to the APEC summit. A fourth Trump-Xi summit in 2026 is expected in December at the US-hosted Group of 20 summit in Miami. In remarks that referred to the initial US trade voyage to China in 1784 to trade American ginseng for Chinese tea, porcelain and silk, Bessent said the US-China relationship would be sustained by “the wisdom – and the will – to recognise where common purpose must prevail over competing interests”. Bessent referred to other trade initiatives agreed during the two previous Trump-Xi summits, including the establishment of a “Board of Trade” to determine mutual tariff cuts on US$30 billion (S$38.45 billion) of non-sensitive goods in each direction, and China’s pledged purchases of US farm goods. A similarly structured “Board of Investment” will provide a structured forum for issues, including market access for American companies in China and “increased predictability for Chinese companies”, he said. He reiterated that the US trade deficit with China remains a source of friction, but the US objective is to “de-risk, not to decouple” from trade with China. REUTERS United States China Trade

articles.title: Trump Taps Palantir Security Chief to Lead National Cyber Agency
articles.content: Michael LoSapio could inherit a depleted workforce and a political headache or two, courtesy of his current employer Carly Page Carly Page Published tue 10 Nov 2026 // 16:15 UTC Make us preferred on Google NHS wants a second opinion on Palantir's glowing self-assessments 5 days ago Feds warn grocers: Don't chill on cyber defenses as freezer hacking spree heats up 6 days ago The White House is apparently a popular residential proxy exit spot 6 days ago Palantir CEO says it's pioneering an antiwar movement – while happily accepting defense dollars 7 days ago NHS counts Palantir benefits at trusts that say they're not using it 8 days ago President Donald Trump has nominated Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA, putting an executive from the controversial government supplier in line to run America's civilian cyber defense agency. The nomination , announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025. LoSapio has served as Palantir's CISO since September 2024 , having previously led the company's infrastructure and network security team. He first joined the data analytics outfit in 2013, later spent a spell at database company SingleStore, and returned to Palantir in 2017. If confirmed, LoSapio would move from securing Palantir's systems to leading the federal government's main civilian cyber defense agency. CISA protects federal civilian networks and works with critical infrastructure operators, including power, water, and telecommunications providers. It's a substantial job, particularly given the state of the agency he would inherit. CISA has shed more than 1,000 staff, roughly a third of its workforce, since Trump returned to the White House, according to  reports . It's now trying to plug the gaps, although acting director Nick Andersen said in September that around 250 would-be recruits were still waiting for security clearance before they could get to work. Andersen has been running CISA since February. With fewer people to go around, CISA is also rethinking where to spend its time. A strategy published last month emphasizes infrastructure whose failure would do the most damage, raising questions about what gets less attention as the agency operates with fewer staff. LoSapio would be the second person Trump has put forward for the role. His previous pick, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April after spending more than a year awaiting confirmation, with his nomination becoming caught up in a dispute involving Republican Senator Rick Scott over Coast Guard contracting. The nomination arrives late in the congressional calendar. If the Senate does not confirm LoSapio before the current Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again for consideration by the incoming Democratic-controlled Senate. Palantir, co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has become a major supplier of technology to US government agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Its work with immigration authorities has attracted criticism from civil liberties groups and Democratic lawmakers concerned about surveillance and the handling of sensitive personal information. The controversy isn't confined to the US either. In the UK,  WhatsApp messages obtained by campaign group Foxglove this week indicate that Palantir privately lobbied a health minister to consider extending its software into GP patient records, despite that data being expressly excluded from its £330 million NHS England contract for the Federated Data Platform. That revelation follows  news that NHS England wants greater oversight of Palantir's claims about the benefits of its software, amid questions over the evidence supporting its performance figures. Those controversies could make LoSapio's confirmation hearings particularly interesting, especially as Democrats prepare to scrutinize Palantir's government business more closely. It's unclear whether LoSapio plans to leave Palantir or what would happen to any financial interests he holds in the company if confirmed. Those are questions likely to come up during a confirmation process that CISA, having spent nearly two years without a permanent boss while losing a third of its workforce, could probably do without dragging on any longer. ® palantir security cisa donald trump Make us preferred on Google

Jeffries, who could become Speaker in the next Congress, said he “strongly supports” chip restrictions in the Senate’s version of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). “We’re going to work hard to make sure that those provisions make it into the final version,” he told reporters at the Capitol on Monday. The bills would allow Congress to block advanced AI chip exports to U.S. foreign adversaries, bar the sale of essential chipmaking tools to countries of concern and require restricted AI chips to have a “location verification mechanism” to ensure they aren’t improperly diverted. They are gaining new momentum after the Nvidia CEO disclosed over the weekend that he had an affair with a woman who U.S. officials concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. The company’s chips are central to the AI boom, powering the technology’s development. As some of the most advanced products on the market, they have often been the focus of U.S. export controls. Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday it was launching an investigation, with a focus on the U.S. national and economic security implications of the incident. Jeffries and several other lawmakers met Monday in the Capitol for a classified briefing with several top administration officials, including Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, and CIA Director John Ratcliffe. While the conversation was primarily focused on Iran, the topic of Nvidia came up, Jeffries noted, saying it’s clear there are “real concerns that need to be addressed.” “What is clear, and the Nvidia issue did come up, [is] that we’re going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened and what the implications are in terms of America’s national security,” he added. articles.title: Grok Agent Exposure Leaks Sensitive SpaceX Rocket Engineering Secrets
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows. The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it. You had one job Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals. “We were shocked,” Claroc said in a Tuesday post . “The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link, and we had never been given it. Had the sales team bought a tool for this, it would have sat behind company sign-in, open only to the team. Built with AI, it went live open to anyone with the link. Claroc notified SpaceXSI of the privacy spill on Sunday. When no one responded, a Claroc official took to X to tag both Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer about the threat. At the time this post went live almost all data remained available with one notable exception: the contents from the 24 SpaceXSI apps. All of them were exposing the information on Monday evening. SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending an email with questions for this article. At the time this post went live, links for all 24 apps returned an “app not found” error. Claroc found sensitive data belonging to other Grok Build users, some working for Fortune 500 companies and a defense contractor. Some of the affected organizations and data revealed includes: A Peruvian construction company: occupational-health dashboard with 3,784 worker medical exams Tesla: service-center scorecard naming 22 technicians with productivity and bonus status A US-Navy ship engineering contractor: roster of 108 people on a Navy logistics support contract A leading luxury cruise company: a galley checklist for a celebrity cruise line listing crew by full name and employee ID A healthcare company: hospital staff app with a roster of about 3,565 employees by name and ID A US IT services company: a confidential proposal to a large retail customer with the hardware bill of materials A Norwegian-Finnish aerospace and defense group: load board and loading procedure for an explosives building at a US plant, plus its HSE training matrix A US home construction company: sales callsheet with about 583 home-buyer prospects, budgets and financing notes A Malaysian holding company: project monitor for 37 developments with profit and sales figures An auto transport company: quote desk with about 4,000 vehicle-transport orders, prices, and margins A US data center colocation and hosting service: confidential IP transit proposal to a European carrier Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he’s in the process of notifying companies. After speaking to the CISO of the luxury cruise company, it “pulled in their whole security team as soon as we shared the findings and are already working to contain the Grok exposure.” A fatal flaw… shared by most other AI platforms Link sharing for Grok Build is intended to streamline the process of developing and deploying apps. A user can input speech or text and have a working app ready for internal testing within minutes. The links are designed to give developers a way to get the app in front of authorized users quickly. The very left of the URLs contain two or more “dice words,” meaning randomly generated phrases such as “failing chassis traders,” although users can modify them. The rightmost portion of the link is grok.me. The URL for an X ads campaign plan was: https://cinder-crane-sand-frost.grok.me. The scheme is intended to prevent links from being easily guessable. When done correctly, a phrase comprising three dice words has roughly 38 bits of entropy, amounting to billions of possible combinations. The idea—sometimes called capability-based access control —is that possession of the URL serves as authorization to the resources behind it. Google has long used this technique to make URLs easy to share but hard to guess. A URL share on that platform might look like: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1BxiMVs0XRA5nFMdKvBdBZjgmUUqptlbs74OgvE2upms/edit There’s a fatal flaw in the way SpaceXSI has implemented the mechanism. Instead of being to the right of the domain—as is the case with Google links—the randomness for Grok Build links is positioned to the left of it. That allows the links to be easily enumerated using passive DNS services. These services monitor central DNS lookup servers. When a server lookup requests the IP address of a previously never-before-seen URL, the transaction is captured in a publicly searchable database. Had Grok followed Google’s approach, the links would have been invisible to passive DNS searchers. Muse, the Meta agent that CEO Mark Zuckerberg said was built from the ground up for security, recently suspended a link-sharing feature after it too was found leaking sensitive data . Aprozper said a passive DNS search returned 43,601 links ending in grok.me. Of them, more than 35,000, or nearly 95 percent, were public, meaning that clicking on the link opened the corresponding app and all data it stored. He said that tests he conducted over the past week showed that, by default, Grok sets links to “Anyone with the link.” Users have the option to change the setting to “invited users” or “only you.” A representative with Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired, said in an email that Grok Build “apps are private by default and nothing goes public unless the creator chooses to share it.” The representative said that competing coding agents from ChatGPT, Lovable, and Bolt also give users the ability to generate shareable links. Aprozper’s tests contradict the representative’s statement. In all cases, Grok Build required users to change anyone with the link to one of the other two options. The Cursor statement regarding other AI coding platforms is correct. Aprozper said that app builders, including Lovable, Bolt, and Replit, “also give each app its own web address, so the same DNS records expose them, too. However, Grok is where we found by far the most sensitive company data.” That means that people using these other platforms are also at risk of exposing sensitive data through shared links. Interestingly, AI platforms that follow the correct sharing link practice include Claude’s published artifacts (claude.ai/public/artifacts/), ChatGPT’s shared conversations (chatgpt.com/share/), and Gemini (gemini.google.com/share/). For all three, the secret randomness is in the path, so DNS never sees it. The representative didn’t respond to follow-up questions, including if SpaceXSI intentionally exposed the proprietary internal information, why the company removed the data after Ars asked about it, and if it planned to notify customers who also exposed similar types of information. Anyone using shareable links with Grok Build should choose the “invite others” option unless they intend to make an app widely available. articles.content: Op de conferenties die onderzoeker Katja Bego sinds 2022 bezocht, trof ze aanvankelijk vooral vertegenwoordigers van ingenieursbedrijven. Die presenteerden bijvoorbeeld nieuwe technieken om data sneller door kabels te sturen, of schepen die kilometerslange geulen kunnen graven voor glasvezelkabels. Ook waren er bedrijven die zich hadden toegelegd op het uitstippelen van nieuwe routes voor glasvezelverbindingen op de zeebodem, of het tekenen van de kaarten ervoor. Zo’n 99 procent van het wereldwijde dataverkeer loopt via zeekabels, die niet dikker zijn dan een tuinslang. „Het is een gesloten industrie”, schetst ze tijdens een gesprek in Amsterdam. „De wereld achter de onderzeese kabels is onzichtbaar, en er was de afgelopen decennia ook weinig belangstelling voor. Ze zijn gewend zichzelf te organiseren. Het woord geopolitiek was lang een soort taboe.” Bego (34) komt uit Amsterdam, maar woont al jaren in Londen. Daar werkt ze voor de geopolitieke denktank Chatham House. Ze heeft zich gespecialiseerd in digitale infrastructuur en de geopolitieke strijd daaromheen. Kort gezegd: het bezit van communicatieverbindingen geeft macht. Dat besef is de afgelopen jaren razendsnel ingedaald. Naarmate de afhankelijkheid van digitale infrastructuur toeneemt, groeit het besef van de kwetsbaarheid ervan. Trok dat schip met zijn anker die kabel nu per ongeluk kapot, of was het sabotage? Berichten over verdachte schepen uit de Russische schaduwvloot en over Chinese vissersboten die wel heel lang op strategische plekken bleven varen, haalden het nieuws. Lees ook Nederlandse zeekabel doelwit van Russisch spionageschip dat eerder sabotage pleegde in de Oostzee Op de conferenties die Bego bezocht, verschenen tussen mensen uit het bedrijfsleven ook steeds vaker militaire uniformen, vertegenwoordigers van geheime diensten en ambtenaren. Geopolitiek werd hoofdonderwerp, beschrijft ze in Deep connections. The hidden battles to control subsea cables , haar recente boek over de strijd om de onderzeese kabelinfrastructuur. Inmiddels is het een verkoopargument als je kunt zeggen dat jouw bedrijf ‘geopolitiek veiliger kabels’ heeft. Dat zijn bijvoorbeeld kabels die niet door de Rode Zee gaan. Er lopen mondiaal zo’n zeshonderd ‘aorta’s van het internet’, leer ik uit uw boek. Van wie zijn die belangrijke glasvezelkabels? „Tot het einde van de Koude Oorlog was er een grote rol voor de staat. De boom -jaren negentig, met de explosieve groei van het internet, veranderden de dynamiek volledig. Toen werd vrijwel alles privaat, en legden bedrijven heel veel kabels. Dat stopte vrij abrupt toen de ‘dotcom-zeepbel’ barstte. „De bedrijven gingen over de kop, maar die zeekabels lagen er. Daar hebben start-ups als Facebook veel profijt van gehad. Voor bedrijven die veel data genereren en de wereld over sturen, was groei heel goedkoop. Ze hoefden zelf weinig te investeren. „Zo’n vijftien jaar geleden kochten de grote techbedrijven die we ‘hyperscalers’ noemen, zich in en begonnen te investeren in zeekabels. Inmiddels zijn zij eigenaar of mede-eigenaar van ruim 60 procent van de kabels, en dat aandeel groeit nog steeds sterk. „Zo legt Meta [het bedrijf achter Facebook, Instagram, Whatsapp en Meta AI] nu een zeekabel van zo’n 50.000 kilometer. Dat wordt de langste en met tien miljard dollar ook de duurste ter wereld; hij omspant en verbindt de hele wereld. In plaats van door de Rode Zee, een strategisch knelpunt, gaat hij onder Zuid-Afrika langs.” Waarom doet Meta zo’n investering? „Het verdienmodel achter kabels is moeilijker geworden. Ze zijn duur om te leggen en het bezit ervan is minder winstgevend geworden. Internet is nu heel goedkoop. Vergelijk de hoeveelheid data voor je telefoon maar met wat je vijf of tien jaar geleden kreeg. Traditionele telecompartijen vinden investeren daardoor moeilijker, vooral in de meest ambitieuze projecten. „Dat is anders voor de echt grote techbedrijven, want die verdienen aan de data, aan advertenties en aan de applicaties die zulke kabels mogelijk maken. Het is voor hen een noodzakelijk kapitaalgoed, net zoals datacenters dat zijn. „Inmiddels kun je de kabels in de praktijk niet meer leggen zonder deelname van die grote bedrijven. Tenzij je het met China doet, dat investeert nog wel. „Over zo’n tien jaar zijn alle oude kabels uit de roulatie. Het risico is groot dat er dan geen trans-Atlantische kabel meer is zonder fors aandeel van Amerikaanse Big Tech. Zo wordt Europa nog afhankelijker van Amerikaanse technologiebedrijven.” Is dat erg? Of moeten we juist blij zijn dat de bedrijven wél investeren? „Enerzijds zorgen de bedrijven dat grote delen van de wereld beter ontsloten worden, zoals Azië en Afrika – China doet dat overigens ook. Maar vergeet niet: infrastructuur is een machtsmiddel. Dat kun je goed zien aan de Britten die in de 19de eeuw vrijwel alle telegraafkabels hadden. Dat gaf ze een enorm overwicht in de wereld. Het huidige equivalent daarvan is de Amerikaanse macht in de digitale economie. En die is vooral in handen van bedrijven. „We hebben het nu veel over de weerbaarheid van het netwerk, waarbij we vooral kijken naar Rusland dat kabels kan saboteren. Maar dit soevereiniteitsaspect is zo mogelijk nog zorgelijker. Want het is heel moeilijk je aan zo’n bezitsstructuur te ontworstelen.” Groot-Brittannië was een koloniale wereldmacht. Maken de huidige verhoudingen de EU een Amerikaanse kolonie? „Kolonie is een te sterk woord, want we hebben er zelf voor gekozen. Maar wel een soort vazalstaat. We hebben soevereiniteit uitbesteed aan een ander land. Nu merken we te weinig bewegingsvrijheid om zelf keuzes te maken, of het nu om toegang tot Starlink gaat of de afhankelijkheid van Amerikaanse software, AI en wapensystemen. „Dat systeem en die afhankelijkheid vonden we in vredestijd wel prima. Nu gebruikt de Amerikaanse overheid die macht in toenemende mate tegen ons, en merken we hoe weinig Europa daar tegenover kan zetten.” Door de AI-ontwikkeling wordt nu enorm geïnvesteerd in datacenters en kabels. Als die AI-bedrijven omvallen, ligt de infrastructuur er nog. Wat denkt u van de vergelijking met de dotcom-zeepbel? „Na die zeepbel, rond de eeuwwisseling, kon veel infrastructuur worden hergebruikt voor andere innovaties. Het maakt voor zeekabels niet uit of ze worden gebruikt om te netflixen of voor bijvoorbeeld geldverkeer, defensie of overheidsdata. En ze hebben een lange levensduur. Maar AI-chips hebben een vrij specifiek gebruik en ze slijten snel. Het is nog maar de vraag wat overblijft als de zeepbel knapt.” Bego belicht in haar boek ook een weinig bekend knelpunt: er is een gebrek aan schepen om kabelbreuken snel te kunnen repareren. Voor Europa en het trans-Atlantische zijn er maar zes. Een strategisch denkende tegenstander zou die reparatieschepen kunnen saboteren. Bego: „De 1,4 miljoen kilometer kabel op de zeebodem kun je niet in z’n geheel beschermen. Je moet dus vooral zorgen dat je kabelbreuken snel kunt repareren. Daar zit een enorme kwetsbaarheid. Het systeem is nu volledig privaat. In vredestijd werkte dat goed en kon je je het veroorloven maar een paar van die schepen te hebben. Maar daar zijn we niet meer. In deze schaduwoorlog voelt het onveilig.” Binnen de NAVO en de EU wordt sinds een paar jaar meer over kabels nagedacht, schetst de onderzoeker. „Maar daarmee zijn knelpunten nog niet opgelost.” Er is dus geen plan en er zijn niet genoeg onderhoudsschepen als kabels worden doorgesneden. Dat is nogal een somber beeld. „De NAVO heeft wel allerlei nieuwe taskforces. En de EU heeft een goed actieplan voor kabelbescherming geschreven. Dat is een grote stap. Maar er zijn ook nog veel plannen niet. Zoals voor uitbreiding van de reparatievloot. Het duurt wel vijf tot tien jaar om zo’n schip te bouwen. En dan moet je de mensen nog trainen. „Binnen landen is vaak al niet duidelijk wie verantwoordelijk is voor de kabelinfrastructuur, laat staan tússen landen. Kabels worden bovendien vaak door meer gebruikers gedeeld. En het zijn bij uitstek dual-use goederen, dus voor zowel militair als civiel gebruik. De NAVO is zelf ook grotendeels afhankelijk van commerciële kabels. „Stel dat de Noordzee een actief oorlogsgebied wordt en er worden veel kabels tegelijk gesaboteerd. Welke kabel repareer je dan als eerste? En stuur je dan een schip van een bedrijf? Of is dat dan niet verzekerbaar? Dat zijn cruciale vragen. Als er nu iets misgaat, hebben we de antwoorden niet. Terwijl het in de afschrikking al helpt als je überhaupt een plan hebt.” Doe eens een voorzetje? Wat moet Nederland nu concreet doen? „Ik heb wel een specifiek idee: die reparatieschepen en -experts zijn nu allemaal particulier. Kun je die mensen reservist laten worden? Zodat je ze in een noodsituatie kunt oproepen? Of kun je marinepersoneel trainen om ook kabels te repareren?” Kun je je toekomstscenario’s voorstellen waarin we internetkabels doorknippen en datacenters nationaliseren? „In oorlogssituaties hoort ‘kabelknippen’ er wel bij. Kabels staan hoog op de lijst van doelwitten. Het is duidelijk dat Rusland plannen maakt om onze kabels door te knippen. „Wij maken natuurlijk ook zulke plannen. Die zijn vooral gericht op Rusland. Ik weet niet of ze er ook zijn voor de trans-Atlantische kabels met Amerika. Zo hoog is de spanning denk ik nog niet opgelopen.” Zou bewust doorknippen van de kabels tussen Europa en Amerika het einde van het internet betekenen? „Als we dat punt bereiken, hebben we waarschijnlijk nog wel grotere problemen. Versplintering van het kabelnet zou een ongewenst bijproduct kunnen zijn van geopolitieke keuzes en machtsvertoon van de belangrijkste spelers in dat netwerk. „Tijdens de Eerste Wereldoorlog gebruikten de Britten hun dominantie in telegraafkabels zó agressief dat het andere landen angst aanjoeg. Daardoor gingen die harder investeren in radiotechnologie, om onder het Britse juk uit te komen. De consequentie was niet alleen dat de Britten hun machtspositie verloren, maar dat ook het netwerk verviel. „Nu zie je iets vergelijkbaars gebeuren. Het goede rentmeesterschap van Amerika lijkt voorbij; het gebruikt zijn machtspositie nu vooral om China uit de systemen te duwen.” Kan Europa daar iets tegenover stellen als alle kabels en datacenters van Amerikaanse of Chinese bedrijven zijn? „Nu de Pax Americana voorbij is en de beschermende rol van Amerika wegvalt, ligt er een kans om een Pax Europeana vorm te geven. Maar dan moet Europa wel investeren in eigen infrastructuur en hoogwaardige technologie. En die moet het beschermen door hard power , militaire macht. Die heeft Europa nog niet. „De ambitie moet nu dus zijn een manier te vinden waarin je weer mee kunt doen. Dat hoeft niet naar Amerikaans model. Macht kan ook gedecentraliseerd zijn. Dat is sowieso zoals Europa werkt.” En zoals het internet werkt? „Ja, precies. Het is geen natuurwet dat je steeds maar twee of drie bedrijven overhoudt voor belangrijke internetfuncties. ” Waar zou u nu een kabel trekken als Europeaan? „Ik ben enthousiast over de plannen bij de Europese Commissie voor het trekken van een kabel onder de Noordpool door. Daarmee kunnen data sneller naar Azië en je vermijdt geopolitieke hotspots. „Het plan is om een directe verbinding te maken met Japan en met Canada, zonder langs Amerika te gaan. Dat kost zo’n 2 miljard euro. Nederland betaalt mee. Het kost veel geld en het is heel geopolitiek, maar het is ook heel symbolisch voor wat wél kan.” Katja Bego: „Er zit een enorme kwetsbaarheid in het snel kunnen repareren van zeekabels.” Foto Merlijn Doomernik Zoom in Maak NRC jouw voorkeursbron op Google Bij Google kan je nu zelf aangeven welke nieuwsbronnen jij vaker wil zien in je zoekresultaten. articles.title: US Uncovers Iranian Sabotage Plot Targeting Nuclear-Capable UK Airbase
articles.content: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The US removed all its bombers from the UK's RAF Fairford base last month after a major incident in September that police described as "suspicious" The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe. The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed. The three men have been accused by the DOJ of being involved in 18 attacks and attempted attacks, including in London, Amsterdam and Paris. Some of the incidents were said to be directed by the men over FaceTime. The DOJ said they acted in the name of the group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI). Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said. The DOJ said that most recently, al-Hassani "orchestrated a terrorist plot" at RAF Fairford - where on 27 September a major incident was declared after suspicious vans were reported near the base. Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident at RAF Fairford. Al-Hassani and Mohajeri were allegedly both in Iran at the time of the incident, the indictment claims. Meanwhile, al-Saadi was coordinating with the pair through third parties from a prison in New York, where he is awaiting trial on previous charges after being arrested in August, it adds. US court records show that al-Saadi is due in court on 19 November, though it is not clear whether this status conference - which is usually a routine scheduled appearance - relates to the new charges or the previous ones. The BBC has asked the Southern District of New York for comment. Image source, Department of JusticeImage caption, Mohammad Ali al-Hassani (left) and Mohsen Mohajeri (right) allegedly planned attacks on London from Iraq Mohajeri and al-Hassani are not in custody, two sources told the BBC's US partner CBS News. The BBC has asked the DOJ for comment on the suspected whereabouts of the two men not in US custody. In the DOJ's statement detailing the indictments, it said: "Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK." It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen". Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year. The indictment also details an arson attack on a Jewish charity in London on 17 April, which allegedly saw al-Hassani "directing" an individual over FaceTime. On 17 April , a building previously used by Jewish Futures, an educational charity, was set alight in Hendon, north-west London. The following day, the DOJ said al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London. On 18 April, Kenton United Synagogue in Harrow was targeted in an arson attack. A 17-year-old boy pleaded guilty to the incident earlier this year. Image source, Department of JusticeImage caption, Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi is currently in prison in New York, awaiting trial for previous charges The indictment also claims the three were involved in attacks on the Bank of New York Mellon building in Amsterdam on 15 March and on the Bank of America building in Paris on 28 March. It added that the trio tried to carry out attacks on "Jewish institutions in the US", including attempting to target a synagogue in Manhattan, New York in March or April. "This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said. He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention. Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Armed police officers were posted outside the RAF Fairford base following the incident in September A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase. No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized. The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot". On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said. In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged. According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel". The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated. "On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base." The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive. "At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route," it added. It was in the very early hours of 27 September, that the vans were spotted by a local farmer who was heading home from a party, and called the police. The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident. Two British nationals appeared in court last month in connection with the alleged Iran-linked plot. The US withdrew all its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident, with President Donald Trump citing "some threats" to the base as the reason. RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades. In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from there to the Middle East for "defensive" strikes on Iran. In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces". articles.title: White House Directs Federal Subsidies Toward Domestic Quantum Foundries
articles.content: Policymakers from Congress and the executive branch are looking for ways to further boost the U.S. quantum computing industry, including by growing industrial capacity to translate scientific breakthroughs into workable technology. Deputy Secretary of Commerce Paul Dabbar said the American industry is “by far the greatest leader in quantum technologies,” with a tech stack that is the envy of the world. The challenge will be translating those technological gains into real, brick-and-mortar industrialization and manufacturing dominance. Dabbar pointed to other examples of federal support, such as grant funding from the CHIPS and Science Act and letters of intent signed earlier this year with nine companies investing more than $2 billion into different quantum technologies. But one of the primary questions that Commerce officials ask companies when making decisions on federal investments is “How do we move a bit further down the road from discovery towards actually supporting individual technologies that can commercialize?” he said. That question is being driven by U.S. assessments that the country’s quantum technology edge is real but is being threatened by countries such as China that have more robust industrial capacity. Dabbar said the federal government is also attempting to follow its own example, citing White House executive orders on quantum computing and more aggressive timelines for agencies to migrate to quantum encryption, measures that CyberScoop was first to report last year. Commerce is the first agency scheduled to deploy its post-quantum encryption. The department also has the authority to place export controls on technologies, as it did for Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable AI models earlier this year. Dabbar expressed caution but suggested Commerce officials were willing to use such controls to advance the interests of American technology makers. “We have to be very careful about American leadership on the frontier on all technologies, and quantum is certainly one of them,” Dabbar said. “We want to be very thoughtful about making certain that which is invented by people in this room are retained by people in this room and are not copied or stolen.” Dabbar’s comments came the same day that the Commission on U.S. Quantum Primacy released a report detailing the major challenges facing the American quantum industry. The report warned that while research, software and private investment are “major strengths” for U.S. industry in its global competition with China, China’s manufacturing and supply chain production threatens to erode that edge. “American scientific strengths may not translate into leadership in deployment and industrial production,” the report stated. Boosting American industrial capacity in quantum is among the report’s top recommendations, including investments in physical infrastructure such as factories, foundries and suppliers that can “turn future breakthroughs into reliable systems.” “To date, many quantum milestones have rightfully been measured in technical and scientific terms,” the report stated. “But national leadership requires a broader ambition: quantum primacy—the ability to turn scientific advances into sustained strategic advantage across quantum technologies.” The commission is due to issue a final report in Spring 2027. Sens. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M. and Todd Young, R-Ind., served as co-chairs of the commission. Meanwhile, Luján pointed to an alleged national security incident involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as evidence that U.S. private industry can’t be trusted to protect America’s tech secrets. According to media reports Huang, who is married, had an affair with Chinese tech executive Alice Huang, later identified by U.S. intelligence agencies as a foreign intelligence asset working for China. When asked about how to maintain U.S. competitiveness in quantum computing and other technologies, Luján said tech executives “need to be smarter” about protecting America’s tech secrets. “People need to make better decisions when you’re entrusted with that kind of power and responsibility,” he said. Luján, who did not mention Huang by name, said tech executives “know that other countries, they send people here to do bad things and get people locked up into telling secrets and things of that nature.” “That clearly happens, and now we’re learning about it and the stock market’s reacting…don’t be stupid,” Luján said. Luján said that while Democrats taking control of Congress will involve efforts to “push back” against executive branch overreach, he is open to working with the Trump administration and Republicans on legislation focused on the workforce and bringing “substantial investments across the United States in this space to ensure that the United States is going to stay in the front” of quantum computing. But he suggested those investments could be wasted if Congress does not intervene with “good policy” and if tech executives can’t self-police their behavior. He pointed to another emerging technology, AI, where an innovation-at-all-costs approach has left industry poorly positioned to deal with cybersecurity and safety concerns. “As we’re learning now from whistleblowers and others from some AI companies that we also need policy and guardrails, and the United States is qualified in a few [of those] areas,” Luján said.

articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Published Nov 11, 2026, 06:33 AM Updated Nov 11, 2026, 06:13 PM Set as preferred source Listen VILNIUS, Nov 11 - NATO scrambled jets overnight after at least four drones strayed into the airspace of the Baltic states during Ukrainian strikes on Russia, officials said on Wednesday, triggering brief alerts to citizens of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia to seek shelter. Ukrainian military drones straying into the airspace of Finland and the Baltics this year have fuelled concern that the Ukraine war is spilling into NATO countries that border Russia and its ally Belarus. There were no reports of injuries on what Lithuania's Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius called "a difficult night". One of the warnings covered Kaunas, Lithuania's second-most populous city, home to about 300,000 people. The incidents occurred on a night that Ukrainian drones attacked Russia's northwest, home to major Baltic Sea export facilities and a big oil refinery, setting afire the Ust-Luga port area and injuring three people. Moscow has accused Kyiv of using NATO airspace as cover for attacks, while Kyiv says Russian signal jamming sometimes sends some of its drones off course. The NATO nations generally blame Russia for such incidents, for igniting the war by invading its neighbour in 2022. Two attempts were made to shoot down a drone over Lithuania but both failed, and it later crossed into neighbouring Latvia's airspace, Lithuanian armed forces Chief of Defence Staff Giedrius Premeneckas told a news conference. "We can only assume some of the drones involved in the attack against Russia were diverted by electronic warfare measures, but there is no confirmed information as to whether the drone was Ukrainian or Russian," Premeneckas said. Finland, another Russian neighbour, adopted temporary airspace and maritime curbs in the eastern Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, its defence forces said on X, but also withdrew them later. "The restrictions were a precautionary measure to ensure the authorities' ability to operate and the safety of bystanders," they added. Drone debris killed two in Russia's Smolensk region bordering Belarus, Russian newswires cited the local governor as saying. TWO-DAY TALKS IN ABU DHABI In Ukraine, an overnight Russian air strike knocked out power in parts of the industrial city Kryvyi Rih, injured one in the second-biggest city Kharkiv and another six in Zaporizhzhia, officials and emergency services said. Reuters could not immediately confirm the reports independently. Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians though both consider energy infrastructure to be valid targets. The turmoil comes against the backdrop of a two-day meeting between Russian and Ukrainian officials in Abu Dhabi from Tuesday, as the United States makes a new push to end their war. As Ukraine attacks Russian oil shipping ports on the Baltic Sea, some of its drones have missed their targets, prompting security warnings in neighbouring countries and even a government collapse this year in Latvia. articles.title: European Digital Fairness Act Criminalizes Exploitative App Interface Architectures
articles.content: The European Commission is set to unveil new rules on Wednesday (11 November) to prevent people from being manipulated by companies and influencers – but digital rights experts have said the legislation doesn’t go far enough. According to a leak of the draft legislation, seen by EUobserver, the Digital Fairness Act (DFA) imposes more controls on how social media influencers can market products, while combatting dark patterns designed to manipulate consumers online. In 2022, an EU Commission study found that 97 percent of the most popular websites and apps used by consumers employed dark patterns – intentional design choices to manipulate users towards choices that are more profitable for companies. The DFA proposal aims to require that social media influencers state sponsorship deals by prominently labelling advertisements using terms such as “advertisement” or “commercial collaboration”, where influencers cannot misrepresent such adverts as a personal endorsement. “People expect that influencers provide genuine advice or tips, not to be quietly sold the latest anti-wrinkle cream or fashionable outfit,” said Agustín Reyna, director general of consumer rights body BEUC . “If someone is promoting products on social media, it should be clearly stated.” The draft also proposes a complete ban on misrepresenting information about products, or sending fake message notifications suggesting someone has been in touch when really, nobody messaged. “Digital markets have for too long left consumers feeling disempowered and frustrated in a maze of complex cancellation processes for subscriptions they do not want, untransparent ticket pricing, or ‘low stock’ warnings that pressure them,” Reyna added. The draft legislation forbids misleading choices about data-sharing or cookies which present refusal as the wrong choice or use deliberately confusing phrases. And the wording of the leaked act also says that cancelling an online subscription should be easy. The DFA proposal would only ban personalised advertising and pricing if likely to cause harm and if the consumer is vulnerable. And it does not set out to ban addictive features like autoplay or infinite scrolling unless users actively switch off these features. “That leaves significant uncertainty and potentially lengthy case-by-case assessments,” said Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, senior policy advisor at rights watchdog EDRi . “Why recognise the problem of addictive design so explicitly without introducing stronger obligations to prevent it?” “Offering an opt-out should not automatically be considered sufficient,” she said.  However, Domínguez de Olazábal called it a “significant step” that “the commission’s proposal creates binding rules against manipulative design, banning fake message notifications, repeated pressure to reverse choices and deliberately complicated refusal mechanisms.” To read this story, log in or subscribe Enjoy access to all articles and 25 years of archives, comment and gift articles. articles.title: House Science Committee Fortifies Federal Research Budgets Against Freezes
articles.content: The incoming Democratic majority on the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology is preparing to wield its new power to conduct oversight of President Donald Trump’s cuts and reshuffling within the federal science and research enterprise. “We’re going to do oversight, and we’re going to take a look at how we can structure legislation in ways that make it more difficult for the Trump administration to continue to do this damage,” said Rep. Zoe Lofgren, who is now poised to lead the committee. In an interview this summer and recent emailed responses following the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections, Lofgren told FedScoop the panel is preparing to dive deeper into controversial Trump administration policies such as to grant cuts at the Department of Energy that targeted blue states , apparent impoundment of funds at the National Science Foundation, an Environmental Protection Agency reorganization that replaced its research office , and political appointees making grant award decisions .  The administration’s actions give the committee — which has oversight of almost the entire federal research enterprise — “a lot to cover,” Lofgren said. While the list of oversight priorities for Democrats may be long, Lofgren and colleagues also have some optimism about legislation in areas that have traditionally had more bipartisan buy-in. Specifically, Lofgren said her priorities will be quantum, fusion, and artificial intelligence.  The House science panel has broad oversight of federal research and science agencies, making it an unavoidable venue for major science and technology legislation. Over the past decade, that’s included bills such as the National Quantum Initiative Act, the CHIPS and Science Act, and the Weather Act Reauthorization.  Politicization within AI might make legislation in that space “tricker,” but the 31-year House veteran said “all three — and certainly fusion and quantum — have always had a bipartisan effort in the House and in the committee.” While Lofgren has previously chaired other House panels, including committees on administration and ethics, the coming Congress would be the first time taking the gavel on the chamber’s science panel. The California congresswoman, whose district includes part of Silicon Valley, has led the Democrats on the committee as the ranking member since 2023. When asked about what the committee might start with, Lofgren said everything she’d pointed to was on the table. “I will stop at nothing to earn back the trust of our allies across the globe, end the brain drain, restore scientific integrity across our agencies, and reaffirm our leadership in science,” Lofgren said. Notably, committee Democrats identified legislation as a possible mechanism for holding the current administration in check. As the second Trump administration has sought to alter what the federal government spends its money on, science funding has been among the targets. Science grants and programs were subject to termination as the administration sought to purge activities related to diversity, equity and inclusion and climate research from the federal government.  Despite Congress mostly rejecting Trump’s deep proposed cuts to science agencies during the last appropriations cycle, the administration has continued to push for significant reductions and, according to analysis by advocates like Grant Witness , appears to be withholding science funds at multiple agencies.  As a result, Lofgren said the committee will be closely looking into legislative levers to prevent the Trump administration’s actions, such as language that’s “more prescriptive on how money is spent,” she said.  “When you have agencies withholding money that Congress instructed them to spend so that they can move it around for their own pet projects, we have to come up with ways to get in front of that sort of blatant corruption so it cannot happen again,” Lofgren said. In an interview speculating about a Democratic-led committee this summer, Rep. Deborah Ross, D-N.C., similarly told FedScoop that a priority would be taking back Congress’s funding authority for science and research by directing how things are done at agencies. “We are going to have to be much more prescriptive with this administration and give them much less discretion about what to do,” Ross said.  A spokesperson for the current committee chair, Rep. Brian Babin, R-Texas, didn’t respond to FedScoop’s requests for comment on strategy or priorities under a Democratic-led panel. In terms of oversight, Lofgren pointed broadly to the impact Trump has had on the science and research ecosystem as a focus. “The Trump administration has taken a real hatchet to the science enterprise in this country,” Lofgren said. “They have illegally defunded research that has been directed by law … in doing so, they have done huge damage to science research and all endeavors. Not only the product of the research, but the pipeline of scientists.” Lofgren said she’s spoken to multiple university leaders about their inability to admit doctoral students and postdoctoral students because they lack the resources to pay for the research. Moreover, she said, policies targeting international students threaten the pipeline of innovators who are Americans by choice.  When asked about priorities for a Democratic-controlled panel this summer, committee member Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., similarly pointed to the need to show the impact of the administration’s choices. “I think it’s important that the American people understand the grievous harm that is being done to the American research establishment during this administration, and that harm will be felt for decades,” said Whitesides, former NASA chief of staff who was the first CEO of Virgin Galactic. People won’t immediately see the impact of the discoveries that would have been made as a result of that funding, but Whitesides said the United States will be lacking, particularly in comparison to international competitors. The administration’s policies, for example, have caused researchers to leave the U.S. for Europe and China , he noted.  In September, Grant Witness and States United Democracy Center launched a tool that estimated $177 billion in federal dollars has been disrupted under the second Trump administration. Those organizations, which used public records to analyze impacted federal funding, concluded that Texas had lost the most federal funding of any state and Vermont lost the most per resident. Also on Lofgren’s radar for oversight: The Trump administration’s push to gain equity stakes in private industry. That includes equity in quantum business and, more recently, stakes in semiconductor supply chain companies. Per a Cato Institute tracker, the Trump administration has made roughly 40 such investments. “I have deep concerns about the government’s growing ownership interest in industry, and it is only compounded by the fact that these seem to be concentrated in certain industries,” Lofgren said. Such a mechanism has only been used in emergency situations in the past and shouldn’t be part of regular business with the government, she said. Lofgren likened the activity of seizing “control of the means of production” to communism and noted that there’s irony given Trump’s frequent comments calling political opponents communists.  “We’re going to have some oversight over that and the impact on the science enterprise,” she said. Some of the possible focuses for Democrats were previewed at a hearing just before the August recess featuring Trump’s top science and tech advisor, Michael Kratsios. The committee members pressed the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy director on various research and science policies, including White House activity in grants decisions at NSF and the agency’s apparent withholding of funds.  Since then, public records obtained by Democracy Forward and shared with FedScoop provided new insight into activities at the agency and, for some, called into question the veracity of Kratsios’ testimony denying White House involvement.  Lofgren’s legislative priorities align with work the committee has already been conducting over the past couple of Congresses, and there’s still a chance legislation that’s already approved by the panel could win passage before the end of the current session. That includes key quantum legislation and multiple AI-related bills.  “We’re still working to get them finished this year, but if not, we would hope to move them next year,” Lofgren said of the legislation. With respect to AI, the committee has advanced a number of bills in the current Congress — including the CREATE AI Act ( H.R. 2385 ), which would formally establish an AI research resource at NSF, and the AI Security and Innovation Act ( H.R. 9363 ), which would codify the AI standards body within the National Institute of Standards and Technology.  On quantum, the committee has approved the National Quantum Initiative Reauthorization ( H.R. 8462 ), which would re-up legislation that established the national strategy for quantum research and development.  Fusion, meanwhile, is beginning to get more attention from the panel, with Lofgren and committee member Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., recently introducing the American Leadership in Fusion Act ( H.R. 10574 ) to advance the energy technology as a source of power that’s free of greenhouse gasses. That bill includes millions in funding for NSF and DOE for fusion work. Lofgren said she intends “to move on that quickly.”  The bill’s Republican co-sponsor is also looking for movement and questioned the Trump administration about its support. In July, Obernolte asked Kratsios about the absence of funding for fusion in Trump’s fiscal 2027 budget request when AI and quantum each received ample support. The OSTP leader said fusion was a priority, citing a goal to be able to demonstrate commercial fusion power by the mid-2030s. Obernolte pointed to the need to work with Congress. “It’s going to require a partnership between Congress and the administration to get that funded, and commercialization is an important part of that strategy,” Obernolte said. Of her three focus areas, Lofgren identified AI as potentially the more difficult to reach agreement on given the divide between Democrats, who are generally pro-regulation, and Republicans, who worry that regulation stifles innovation.  But she said the committee “can regulate and innovate at the same time, just as we always have.” At the same time, there’s also interest in centralizing the chamber’s AI work under a single committee, which could change each panel’s share of issues involving the technology. According to reporting from Politico in September, Democratic leaders in the House are weighing an AI select committee. That effort is reportedly being led by Reps. Bill Foster of Illinois and Ted Lieu of California, and if advanced, may require some committee leaders to give up jurisdiction of AI issues. Foster spoke to FedScoop about why the House should create a committee to deal with AI this summer. The particle physicist-turned-congressman noted that Obernolte, who co-chaired the temporary House Task Force on AI in 2024, had tried to make the case for turning that group into a select committee but ran into seven committee chairs who all wanted their panel to be doing AI. A full standing committee, he noted, is what most other countries have.  “We got to get past this,” Foster said. “And frankly, if you’re interested in whether the Democrats are going to be doing something serious about AI, look to see if they’re willing to put in place in Congress an organization capable of dealing with it.”

articles.title: Fireworks AI Suffers Cascading Customer Secret Exposures in Repeat Breach
articles.content: Inference biz pins latest breach on cloud provider and LLMJacking miscreants Connor Jones Connor Jones Cybersecurity reporter Published tue 10 Nov 2026 // 15:28 UTC Make us preferred on Google 2013 breach at Russian cybercrime forum resurfaces with millions of victims' credentials 9 hours ago Shipping giant Maersk probes 'IT security incident,' data theft 11 hours ago OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models 17 hours ago November Patch Tuesday boasts over 1,000 bugs, one already under attack 1 day ago Ring robots ready to patrol paranoids’ pads 1 day ago Fireworks AI has disclosed another cyberattack in October and a wider customer data exposure involving billing records, datasets, and incomplete model weights. The company, which lets customers train and run AI models, said a third-party cloud provider hosting its research and development machines was compromised on October 23. Attackers used that access the following day to reach Fireworks development systems and run an unauthorized workload. Fireworks suspects links to financially motivated criminals involved in LLMJacking – selling unauthorized access to AI models through illicit gateways. Fireworks grouped the affected data into three categories: Resource metadata: Resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, creation times, and more Billing information: Billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment histories, account balances, and credit usages. Payment card numbers are not saved and therefore unaffected Model weights and datasets: For certain customers, a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets were accessed, Fireworks said Lin Qiao, Fireworks co-founder and CEO, said the apparent motive was not stealing model weights in response to concerns raised by Cantina Security CEO Hari Mulackal. "From what we see attackers are not after weights," said Qiao. "Most downloads were partial and stopped." Render founder and CEO Anurag Goel shared a notification from Notion warning that some chats with its AI assistant may have been exposed through the Fireworks incident. "Following an investigation by the Notion security team, we have determined that your workspace, Render, was among the <1 percent of Notion workspaces that may have been affected by the Fireworks security incident," the email sent to Goel stated. "Some unattributable chat sessions with Notion AI may have been exposed in this incident." Notion said the exposed transcripts lacked separate information linking them to particular users or workspaces. As Reddit users pointed out , however, the conversations themselves could contain identifying details. "Beyond what's in the chat transcript itself, there's no information tying the chat back to your workspace, users, or company," the email added. "No other data from within your workspace is affected." Bloomberg reports that Fireworks is also working with customers including Cursor and Harvey to assess the impact. Fireworks' update confirmed that it worked with Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 team to remediate the attack, which included rotating credentials, isolating affected systems from the network, and tightening up data storage access and monitoring systems. The update did not state how many customers were affected by either of the two attacks in October. Fireworks first disclosed an incident on October 9  after detecting unauthorized use of internal credentials on October 6. Attackers accessed environment variables in evaluation jobs, including API keys and tokens belonging to some customers. At the time, Fireworks said it had found no evidence of access to models, datasets, training data, inference traffic, or personal information. Monday's update substantially broadens the disclosed impact. ® ai security cyber-crime data breach Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: Congressional Leaders Demand Bipartisan Mandates on Quantum and AI
articles.content: Stay Connected Featured eBooks Health Technology: Relaunch of VA EHR Read Now Law Enforcement Technology Read Now Insights & Reports By Grace Dille , Technology Reporter, Nextgov/FCW | November 10, 2026 05:35 PM ET Republican Rep. Pat Harrigan of North Carolina said he expects political headwinds for emerging technologies, while Democratic Sen. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico urged Congress to work together to sustain U.S. leadership in quantum. Quantum Computing Artificial Intelligence Congress Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., and Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., called for bipartisan cooperation to advance emerging technologies Tuesday, though they emphasized their differing priorities for maintaining U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence and quantum computing. Speaking at the Special Competitive Studies Project’s AI+ Quantum Summit in Washington, D.C., the lawmakers both stressed the importance of getting tech policy right in the next Congress. Harrigan advocated for a hands-off approach to emerging technologies, while acknowledging that political disagreements over the government's role could create significant challenges after elected officials are sworn in on Jan. 3. “To be totally honest, I expect a lot of headwinds in the next Congress,” Harrigan said, adding that conservatives will likely be “playing defense next year.” The Republican pointed to the election of moderate Democrats in both chambers as a potential opportunity for bipartisan cooperation, saying he hopes lawmakers can find common ground to keep government “hands off nascent and emerging technologies as much as possible.” In a separate conversation at the event, Luján stressed that Congress must work together to advance quantum policy and ensure federal policies support scientific progress. “Compromise is not a bad word,” he said. “We have to work together to find some commonality here as well.” “Policy can get in the way,” Luján added. “Is policy going to support future scientific advancements and discoveries, or is policy going to get in the way?” Luján’s remarks came as the Commission on U.S. Quantum Primacy, convened by the Special Competitive Studies Project, released a report Tuesday that identified sustained federal investment in foundational quantum research as a near-term priority. The commission is co-chaired by Luján and Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind. Luján said upcoming federal funding decisions will help determine the country’s direction in quantum, noting that there will be another continuing resolution vote soon. The current continuing resolution funds the government through Dec. 11. “Budgets are a reflection of our priorities, and in the United States, are we going to make substantial investments and lift up our national labs, the ecosystem around how we can strengthen and advance quantum in the United States, or not?” Luján said. “I really believe that that is going to determine what we will do here.” Similarly, Harrigan said Washington needs to support the people and organizations building emerging technologies, including quantum and AI. “Congress needs to do a better job of making sure our research investments translate into something useful, and that's going to take a commitment that lasts longer than anyone in Congress or this administration,” Harrigan said. “We’ve got to give our national laboratories, our universities and private industry some consistency while holding ourselves accountable to the results,” he added. “I don’t think that this is something that ought to divide Republicans and Democrats.” Share This:
