articles.content: La saturation progressive du sens de la vue par les écrans a ouvert un nouvel espace à l’ouïe, jusque-là essentiellement sollicitée par la voix humaine et la musique. Diffusés en ligne, chuchotements et sons de contact amplifiés permettent de nouer avec certaines personnes un rapport très particulier. Un homme apparaît sur un fond noir, devant une toile posée sur un chevalet. Le sourire affable, il s’adresse aux téléspectateurs comme s’il les connaissait chacun personnellement : « Hi, welcome back, I’m glad to see you » (« Salut, content de vous revoir ici »). Il s’emploie alors à peindre montagnes, couchers de soleil ou fermes sous la neige. Le patient professeur conseille et encourage d’une voix douce l’élève invisible. « The joy of painting » (« La joie de peindre ») est un programme télévisé américain, animé par Robert (« Bob ») Ross et diffusé entre 1983 et 1994. Personne, sans doute, n’aurait pu prédire que les méandres d’Internet lui donneraient une seconde célébrité quelques décennies plus tard, ni qu’il deviendrait le modèle de l’ASMR. Ce sigle — pour autonomous sensory meridian response, « réponse sensorielle autonome culminante » en français — désigne une sensation, voire un sentiment suscité par ces contenus, et par extension ces contenus eux-mêmes. Une étiquette apposée sur certaines vidéos reprenant les codes des émissions de Bob Ross : douceur de la voix, lenteur de l’élocution, adresse directe au spectateur et amplification exagérée de certains bruits d’ordinaire peu perceptibles — en l’occurrence, celui du pinceau. Grâce à des micros placés tout près de la source sonore, les créateurs accentuent les sons produits par des objets manipulés : une vidéaste met de la mousse à raser sur un micro, découpe avec des ciseaux une balle antistress à paillettes pour en répandre le contenu. Les séquences mettent souvent en scène une personne « guide » qui, explique l’artiste et chercheuse Alice Lenay, « fait mine de prendre soin du “récepteur” ». Ce « prendre soin » s’incarne dans un jeu de rôle : le ou la vidéaste est une librairie qui te conseille des livres ; une esthéticienne qui te prodigue un soin du visage, etc. Les sons amplifiés exacerbent sa respiration, ses bruits de bouche ; ils mettent mal à l’aise certaines (…) En cliquant sur « S’inscrire », je reconnais avoir pris connaissance de la politique de confidentialité du Monde diplomatique et des droits dont je dispose sur mes données personnelles.

articles.title: Software Engineers Devise Blinding Defenses Against Autonomous Coding Agents
articles.content: A poke in the AI with a sharp stick Thomas Claburn Thomas Claburn AI AND SOFTWARE REPORTER Published tue 10 Nov 2026 // 20:35 UTC Make us preferred on Google AMD winds up Zen 6 cores for faster clock speeds 1 day ago A closer look at Verano, AMD's first step toward a Zen-based superchip to rival Nvidia's Vera Rubin 1 day ago Fireworks AI gets burned twice as customer data exposure widens 1 day ago Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session 2 days ago PyTorch 2.15 tackles the 'one bad GPU' problem 5 days ago Now that LLMs can help analyze commercial software binaries and recreate their functionality, one software developer and student has created a project designed to make this process more difficult. Timo Zhang's  project is called Blind LLM Agents (BLA), and as its name suggests, it attempts to interfere with efforts by AI agents to scrutinize app code. "Coding agents can reverse-engineer shipped packages, CLIs, and WASM in minutes," Zhang told The Register in an email. "Classic obfuscation was built for humans and static tools, not LLMs that reason about meaning. Blind LLM Agents is a protection layer for that threat model." Such agents can also help developers build alternatives to existing commercial software. Last month, Artcraft , a two-person development shop, released seven open-source apps that aim to be replacements for Adobe's commercial apps Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro. Artcraft claims these apps are "clean-room reimplementations" written from scratch in Rust using Anthropic Opus 5.5.  Setting aside the question of whether enlisting an AI model to reimplement an app really immunizes the creator from legal risk, those making apps face the possibility that someone will have an LLM probe published app binaries and reconstruct them through reverse engineering. There's in fact a framework for this, Reverse Engineer Anything (REA). Zhang has faced some criticism on social media for creating a limited barrier to copying other people's work (which at this point might simply be the work of another LLM). But not everyone accepts that all publicly accessible binaries should be easily available for review and reuse. BLA cannot prevent committed reverse engineering efforts, but it may add a bit of friction to the process when LLMs are involved. "It doesn't write app code — it hardens what you've already built," Zhang said. "A transform pipeline (plus MCP tools / an agent Skill) applies renaming, lane splitting, seed-derived string encryption, build polymorphism, WASM export renaming, decoys, self-seal integrity checks, and a coverage matrix that won't claim protection it can't prove. Behavior stays equivalent; recovery cost goes up." Zhang said various evaluations like red teaming and CrackMe challenges to recover keys or flags from hardened artifacts show that BLA is effective.  "We also drive REA (a reverse-engineering agent) against those builds," he said. "Fail-to-break is the pass. CI tracks defense score, self-verifies integrity coverage, and checks functional equivalence. We raise the cost — we don't claim it is unbreakable." The project website says as much, noting that it raises the effort for analysis and adds decoy code, but doesn't promise protection against traditional interactive reverse engineering tools like Ghidra or Frida. Zhang said he's aware of other software projects that aim to interfere with AI, such as Poison Fountain for poisoning training data and Anubis for deterring bots and scraping. BLA, he said, is different. It's for hardening shipping code against reverse engineering and LLM-aided analysis. ® ai ai and ml reverse engineering Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: Critical Infrastructure Operators Revert to Air-Gaps Against Cyberattacks
articles.content: The recent reports of artificial intelligence agents gone rogue —hacking into corporate systems without being told to by the humans who manage them—are enough to make any systems administrator’s hair stand on end. The increasingly powerful abilities of frontier and other advanced AI models, combined with the apparent inabilities of their creators to keep them caged, have only added to the worries of companies already wrestling with how to protect themselves against AI -armed attackers. Cybercriminals of all kinds are using AI tools in much the same way legitimate organizations do, boosting their productivity and moving their operations from human to machine speed. Meanwhile, businesses have understandably embraced AI themselves. But every new AI tool or application a company chooses to roll out comes with its own security risks. When it comes to AI, many companies feel like they have to take an “adopt or die” business perspective, says Leslie Nielsen , executive vice president and chief information security officer at Mimecast. “They think everybody’s going to pass them by,” Nielsen says. “But then the other side is, if you adopt too fast, it’s adopt and die, right?” While AI threats may be rapidly advancing , so are AI-powered defenses. And experts say following old-school best practices can go a long way toward protecting against even the most advanced attackers. The tactics used by AI attackers aren’t a whole lot different from those of human-powered adversaries, they’re just faster and more efficient, Nielsen says. As a result, the fundamentals of defense don’t need to be much different either. “It’s all the basic stuff you should be doing anyway,” he says. “It just becomes more important because the attacks are faster and the attacks are cleaner and more successful sometimes.” That means making sure that access to sensitive data is limited to those who actually need it; immediately patching security vulnerabilities when they become known; and making sure that all critical data is backed up and accessible if needed. And of course, follow the absolute basics, like making sure your cybersecurity defenses require strong passwords and multifactor authentication, and that you’re screening for phishing emails. Just like the attackers, defenders need to bolster themselves with AI tools to speed up their responses, Nielsen says. He added that this is especially true for small- and medium-size businesses that are probably working with smaller security teams. Complicating this already hefty task is the ability of advanced AI models to chain together low-level vulnerabilities into previously undiscovered exploits that could be used to breach a system, says Simon Jelley , vice president of product management at Dell Technologies. “But those risks have always been there,” Jelley says. “It’s just accelerating those exposures and also making AI ultimately smarter.” The AI tools used by companies can end up being the insider threats that no one thinks about, experts say. In the case of the AI models gone rogue, it appears they weren’t trying to do anything malicious, just accomplish the objectives set out by their human creators at all costs. “The difference between AI and a person is AI is the eager intern that’s going to do what you ask, but it’s going to keep working 24-seven to get it done, and it’s going to do everything it needs to do,” Nielsen says. That could include doing things like digging up login credentials and accessing data it shouldn’t, potentially putting that data at risk of exposure. That’s why it’s important that there are guardrails in place to keep AI agents on task and to limit their access to sensitive data. But sometimes companies prioritize productivity over safety, Darktrace president and CEO Ed Jennings says. “You want AI to do all those things that you want employees to do,” Jennings says. “The problem is, a lot of times those agents are given unfettered access. You have to start to watch their behavior.” Companies should also create acceptable use policies for their AI tools, just like they do for other kinds of technology. Jennings notes that employee use of AI agents for personal reasons isn’t just a security risk, it can also get expensive if humans start burning through tokens. While traditional perimeter defenses can help keep attackers out, they don’t do anything to spot or stop them if they do get in. And given the increasing volume and sophistication of AI-powered attacks, experts say it’s more of a question of when, rather than if, companies will be breached. Jennings says that’s one of the reasons his company has focused on behavioral detection for more than a decade. Darktrace’s products were originally designed to spot attackers inside systems by looking for anomalies in human user behavior. Now they’re being used to flag the same kind of signs in AI activity. “AI doesn’t think in terms of boundaries,” Jennings says. “These agents don’t stop at the email layer. They don’t stop at the network layer. They just move laterally. They move freely. They do whatever is necessary and figure out how to do that very quickly.” Jelley, of Dell, says companies have come to realize that they can’t just say that they want to protect everything, because that’s not realistic. Instead, they’re better off identifying their core operations and data and creating a plan for getting them back up and running should an incident occur. “Ultimately, it’s about whether you have a mitigation plan in place to fall back on, a resilient infrastructure that you put in place to recover should the attack happen,” he says. —Bree Fowler This article originally appeared on Fast Company ’s sister website, Inc.com. articles.title: Viral Algorithmic Tourism Forces Amsterdam Into Municipal Gridlock Battles
articles.content: De TikTok-rijen in de Amsterdamse Runstraat voor patat met truffelmayo of Parmezaanse kaas hoeven niet weg. De rechtbank Amsterdam oordeelde dinsdag dat de gemeente Amsterdam de vergunning van Fabel Friet terecht heeft verlengd. De rechtszaak, die sinds 2024 loopt, was aangespannen door buurtbewoners van de 9 Straatjes , die in september tegenover de gemeente in de rechtbank stonden. De omwonenden menen dat de friettent dusdanige overlast, verkeersonveiligheid en rondslingerend afval veroorzaakt, dat de gemeente de vergunning moet intrekken. De rechtbank vindt dat omwonenden onvoldoende hebben bewezen dat sprake is van ontoelaatbare overlast. Wel wordt aangenomen dat het „druk” is rondom de frietzaak, dat veel afval op straat ligt en de toeloop van klanten gevaar kan opleveren voor de verkeersveiligheid. Maar, zo beargumenteert de rechtbank, Fabel Friet is gevestigd in een druk gedeelte en ook andere horecazaken in de buurt hebben wachtrijen. Daardoor komt de ervaren overlast niet alleen of voornamelijk door Fabel Friet en hoefde de gemeente de verlenging van de vergunning niet te weigeren. Lees ook In een langlopende rechtszaak rond de frietzaak willen buurtbewoners af van de TikTok-rijen: ‘Alles in de buurt ademt Fabel Friet’ Fabel Friet, sinds 2020 actief in de Runstraat en daarna op meerdere locaties, ging viraal in 2022. Daarna ontstonden in de al drukbezochte straat zogenoemde ‘TikTok-rijen’, onder meer bestaande uit mensen die via sociale media van Fabel Friet hebben vernomen. De eigenaren van de zaak probeerden sindsdien de overlast tegen te gaan met schoonmaakrondes, ‘crowdmanagers’ om klantenstromen in banen te leiden en de vermeende inzet van een valk om meeuwen te verjagen. Het stelde de omwonenden niet tevreden. De gemeente erkende in september ter zitting dat de leefbaarheid in de buurt rond Fabel Friet onder ‘enorme druk’ staat De rechtbank benoemt dat de gemeente in het centrum voor een lastige balanceeract staat, met de belangen van omwonenden, ondernemers en de leefbaarheid – die allemaal worden beïnvloed door het toerisme . De gemeente erkende in september ter zitting dat de leefbaarheid in de buurt rond Fabel Friet onder „enorme druk” staat, maar dat Amsterdammers ook moeten kunnen ondernemen. Het balanceren is niet afgelopen met deze uitspraak. Die gaat namelijk over een vergunning uit 2024, die inmiddels is verlopen. Sinds 26 april geldt een nieuwe vergunning met aangescherpte regels voor Fabel Friet, waar zowel omwonenden (regels niet streng genoeg) als de frietzaak zelf (vergunningstermijn niet lang genoeg) bezwaar tegen hebben aangetekend bij de gemeente. Daarmee komt de gemeente opnieuw voor de vraag te staan: kan de overlast door de TikTok-rijen bij Fabel Friet wel of niet door de beugel?
